comment:
I support the Environmental Protection Agency's regulation of 1—bromopropane (1–BP). The chemical has health risks, such as damage to the liver and kidneys, cancer, reproductive toxicity, and neurotoxicity. It’s used mainly in dry and industrial cleaning which disproportionately impacts the workers. Limiting its use is for the safety of workers and reduction of long-term exposure.

Scientific research from the National Toxicology Program (NTP) demonstrates that long-term exposure to 1-BP can lead to headaches and cognitive impairment. Even low exposure to 1-BP can lead to irreversible effects, making the regulations critical. Also, the American Public Health Association (APHA) has found that 1-BP exposure caused reproductive harm to women working in industries with the presence of the chemical. The findings show a need to implement safety protocols and phase out the use of 1-BP.

I applaud the EPA for taking appropriate steps to research and regulate 1-BP. Implementing safety protocols and phasing out the chemicals will help protect exposed workers.

comment:
I support the EPA's plan to gradually ban the industrial and commercial use of bromopropane. This chemical is in a plethora of different products that people come into contact with everyday like cushioning, flavoring, cleaners, and aerosols (“Environmental Defense Fund”). However, according to the New Jersey Department of Health, the exposure limit for bromopropane is 10 ppm (“Hazardous Substance Fact Sheet”). With all of these products that contain bromopropane, it is not hard to imagine how someone could easily go over that exposure limit especially if they work in a factory that manufactures products with bromopropane. Furthermore, the Department of Health and Human Services conducted experiments that showed bromopropane causes tumors to appear in animals. This led to it being classified as “reasonably anticipated to be a human carcinogen.” Bromopropane has also been observed to damage people’s nervous systems and even hospitalized people who suffered prolonged exposure (“ToxFAQs”). I do not wish to live surrounded by a chemical that is a potential carcinogen and neurotoxin. That’s why I support the EPA’s conclusion that bromopropane “presents an unreasonable risk.”

comment:
I am in favor of new regulation of 1-Bromopropane (1-BP) by the EPA. I personally lean towards the protection of the health of the general population, regardless of the impacts it may have on private business. If there is a substance or practice found to be universally dangerous, I would like to see action taken to have it regulated in some fashion. This case is one that I find especially dangerous, therefore I agree with the EPAs proposal for new regulation of 1-BP.

The new regulation would prevent consumer access, which is necessary considering nobody needs such a dangerous chemical. Such a chemical should not be in the hands of consumers considering its effects on health. This regulation would also restrict commercial use, and protect any workers that may be around it. This also is a reasonable regulation considering the proposal still allows for the use of 1-BP, just with some conditions. Plus, the proposal also allows for a reasonable transition period where the use of this chemical is banned.
There was a prior comment on this regulation that made a fair argument that whatever chemical may be used as a replacement could potentially be just as dangerous. To that I ask, does the potential danger of the future outweigh the immediate danger of the present? We know that 1-BP has been associated with severe neurotoxicity according to work done in the department of neurology at the University of Michigan. Also, 1-BP causes damage to DNA according to scientists at the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health. Therefore I am in favor of the proposed regulation by the EPA.

Majersik JJ, Caravati EM, Steffens JD. Severe neurotoxicity associated with exposure to the solvent 1-bromopropane (n-propyl bromide). Clin Toxicol (Phila). 2007;45(3):270-6. doi: 10.1080/15563650701226218. PMID: 17453879.

comment:
Metal finishing job shops often employ vapor degreasing to remove surface contaminants prior to metal finishing. As they are job shops, there is wide variability in part configuration, base material composition, and surface contaminant. Few solvents currently exist that are able to remove a wide range of organic contaminants (such as dirt, metal work fluids, rust inhibitors, etc.) from metal surfaces. Most of these solvents (such as methylene chloride (MC) and trichloroethylene (TCE)) are in the process of being banned under TSCA. N-propyl bromide (npb or 1-bromopropane) was an alternative cleaning solvent facilities were encouraged to use as a replacement for MC and TCE. Pursuing a complete ban of npb under TSCA, especially when EPA determined risk mitigation was feasible, would be an undue hardship to metal finishing job shops located in the U.S.

Nearly all of the proposed requirement deadlines key off the publication date of the final rule in the Federal Register. This timing appears inconsistent with most other EPA regulations, which establish deadlines based upon a final rule's effective date. For clarity and consistency purposes, it's recommended all deadlines established in any final rule under TSCA be based upon the effective date of the final rule itself (not its publication date).

OSHA was established to protect workplace health. Instead of "recreating the wheel", increasing regulatory burden, creating compliance uncertainty, and over-reach on the part of EPA, details of PPE requirements for respiratory and dermal protection (e.g., proper respirator selection and fit testing, proper glove selection, training, etc.) should not be called out in EPA's rule under TSCA; rather, EPA should incorporate by reference OSHA's existing regulations as applicable.

EPA should consider outlining periodic exposure monitoring requirements (i.e., ECEL compliance) under TSCA to be analogous to NESHAP compliance monitoring schedules (e.g., Once two (2) consecutive non-initial monitoring results are below the ECEL action level, facility must repeat periodic monitoring at least once every five (5) years. Should non-initial monitoring results show the ECEL or ECEL action level is exceeded, monitoring frequency should return to X-months or Y-months, respectively. Periodic monitoring frequency can return to once every five (5) years should two consecutive monitoring results be below the ECEL action level.)

EPA should not knee-jerk treat a laboratory result of non-detectable as an exceedance of npb's ECEL. Since the goal of this rule is to reduce npb exposure, non-detectable results should be lauded as successful implementation by the regulated facility. To address EPA's concerns, a minimum detection limit could be established instead. Laboratory results reported as non-detectable where the detection limit was above the minimum detection limit established in the final rule could potentially be deemed unacceptable if compliance with the ECEL action level could not be determined. In those cases, facilities may need to repeat exposure monitoring, with 30-days (from the date of determination, not prior exposure monitoring) being a reasonable timeframe. Similarly, EPA should not treat an equipment fault during air monitoring as an exceedance of the npb ECEL. Facilities should be given 30-days (from the determination of an equipment fault) to repeat exposure monitoring. In cases where the condition of use is sporadic, facilities should be allowed more than 30-days to repeat npb exposure monitoring as long as the basis for the delay is adequately documented and maintained in their compliance record.

There is no need to require industrial users of npb to maintain any records beyond what is required to document compliance with the final rule.

EPA proposed 18-month and 21-month deadlines for supplier notification via SDS. Yet EPA's proposed milestone deadlines for industrial uses of npb were all 12-months or less. End users of proprietary, specialty products can very well be unaware of the presence of npb and its accompanying requirements under TSCA. How can a facility be held accountable when they were ignorant of a requirement? By extension, it could be deemed facilities using commodity npb were placed at a competitive disadvantage due to the cost of compliance effectively being in place one to two years prior to those using specialty/proprietary products. To level the competitive playing field, compliance milestone deadlines (e.g., exposure monitoring, WCPP, training, etc.) should all occur after the supplier notification deadline.

Facilities should be allowed to pursue ventilation/exhaust options as a method for npb ECEL compliance. Associated air emissions of npb (and any accompanying public exposure risk) should be regulated by the Clean Air Act, not TSCA. If a facility complies with federal, state, and local air regulations, their npb air emissions should not be banned under TSCA.
